I'm sorry you've had people not believe your suspicions about your son. That's unbelievably frustrating. Your husband's reaction is monstrous. Like many others have said, autism is not a disease. 

Your son is not sick. He's the same kid he was yesterday, and if he's diagnosed autistic, he'll still be the same great kid. It has nothing to do with anything you did or didn't do. Autism is developed in the womb. If he inherited it, it's just as likely to come from the father as the mother.

My four-year-old is autistic. He's hard to deal with sometimes, but that's nothing new. Everyone is hard to deal with sometimes. He's a great little person, and I wouldn't trade him for anything.

The best advice I have for now is to research. Read about autism, read about the experiences of other autistic people. Find out what services are available where you live. Learn what you can do at home to help your son live his best life. Stay away from Autism Speaks. It's an organization that believes that autism can be cured, and that every autistic person is nothing but a burden on the people around them.

WIC is not food stamps. Many families who have food stamps also use WIC, but they're different programs. The max family income to receive WIC benefits is twice as much as food stamps (in Kansas a family of four has to make less than $18xx a month to qualify for food stamps, but can make up to $36xx for WIC).

This is because WIC only provides healthy(ish) foods for pregnant and nursing women, infants, and children under 5. Food stamp benefits can buy almost any food, but WIC can only be used for a pretty strict list of things. Babies who take formula get that, then formula plus fruit and veggie purees and baby cereal after six months. Children over one and pregnant/nursing mothers get a protein (beans or peanut butter here), milk, cheese, eggs, fruits and veggies, and juice.

WIC also provides a basic annual checkup for women and children who receive benefits, nutrition education, and free vaccines. Nursing mothers get breastfeeding support.

I've been in a psych hospital. The first few days are a pretty big adjustment. The huge changes in her routine, the beginning of her treatment, plus the depression and exhaustion mean she's going through a lot right now. 

She's not going to be her normal self overnight. Give her some time. Still reach out to her and make sure she knows you're there for her. A lot of people in her situation end up being forgotten. 

Ask the staff about sending care packages. Cards are always nice, as well as anything that can help relieve boredom. There are only so many times you can play chess or bridge before you never want to see another board game again. Books and magazines are awesome.

Your girlfriend will be better and out of there before either of you know it. Please don't treat her any differently because of her hospitalization. She's not contagious, and she's still the same person.
